utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Please read aloud the affirmation shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Djurdjic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, could you please state your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Momir Stojanovic. I was born on the 12th October, 1958, in Djakovica, the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on, I would kindly ask you the following: Given that we use the same language, please pause briefly before answering so as to enable the interpreters to interpret everything and so that we would have a transcript that would reflect accurately our conversation. General, in the Milutinovic case, you testified before this Tribunal, and in the course of your proofing for today's testimony, you were able to review that transcript. If asked the same questions today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have D010-2614, which is the transcript under seal, have admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00723 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, D011-2687 is the redacted version of this transcript. I seek to tender that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00724.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will acquaint you with the summary of this witness's testimony now. The witness was born in 1958 in Djakovica. Between 1998 and 1999, the witness was head of the intelligence service of the Pristina Corps Command. He will testify about the organisation, competencies, purposes, and tasks of the military intelligence, focusing on the work and competencies of the security department in 1998 and 1999. He will testify about the engagement of military intelligence and military police units of the Pristina Corps in investigating and criminal procedures in co-operation what other bodies and services active on the territory pursuant to instructions, method, and means of operation. He will also explain their co-operation with other state bodies and relevant institutions. He will explain the relationship between the intelligence sector of the Pristina Corps and the military corps -- police units of the Pristina Corps. He will testify about the security section units, as well as the subordinate commands undertook preventative measures in keeping with the orders of the Pristina Corps Command concerning crimes committed by members of the VJ in the subordinate units, as well as prosecuting civilians who committed criminal offences against the Army of Yugoslavia. He will testify about the number of criminal reports submitted during the war for different types of crime, and that there were -- there was a number of on-site investigations undertaken and under the direction of the intelligence section of the Pristina Corps. He will speak about the genesis of the terrorist movement in Kosovo with a particular accent on 1998 and 1999, and the refusal of the leadership of the Albanian separatist movement to accept numerous calls of the Government of the FRY in the Republic of Serbia in order to resolve the political -- the conflict in Kosovo by political means. He will also testify about the choice the terrorist forces chose to use violent means to be successful in seceding Kosovo and Metohija from the rest of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia. The witness will also testify about the knowledge and information that point out to the links that existed between the terrorist forces and the Kosovo Verification Mission and the abuse of authority by the Kosovo Verification Mission as well as co-operation between the KVM and NATO forces and the Siptar terrorist movement. He will also explain the causes of migration for the -- of the population of Kosovo and Metohija in the abuse of civilians by the KLA and the Albanian separatist movement as a whole. He will also testify about the crimes of the KLA committed against Albanians who were loyal to the FRY and the Republic of Serbia and other non-Albanian population. He will testify about the engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia in protecting human life and property and securing safety of military traffic, maintaining order and discipline in the VJ. This witness will testify about the superior commands of the General Staff of the VJ and the 3rd Army, carried out inspections and control of the intelligence section of the Pristina Corps. He will specifically address control carried out in the intelligence section undertaken by a number of personnel from the security administration of the General Staff, in particular, by General Vasiljevic between the 1st and 7th of June, 1999. He will describe the meeting of the 1st of June, 1999, in the Grand Hotel in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, General, can you tell us briefly what is it that you do nowadays?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am a retired general of the Army of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Briefly tell us, please, what were your most important positions in the VJ up until 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at all the positions there are in the military security service. That is to say, the chief of security in the regiment, in a division, in a corps, in the counter-intelligence group. My position was also that of director of the military security service of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro. I also performed command tasks and duties of brigade commander as well as Chief of Staff of a corps and representative of the deputy commander of the land forces of the Army of Serbia Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998 and 1999 until the end of the war, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 until the end of the war, I was head of the security section in the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what is the role of military security organs within the command system of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Military security service organs are professional organs of the competent commands and institutions of the army tasked with counter-intelligence and general security protection provided to the respective units and institutions as well as their commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What are the competencies of the military security service?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The organs of the military security service in keeping with Article 30 on the Army of the FRY have the rights, duties, and authority accorded to an organ of the Ministry of the Interior but only inside the framework of the Army of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who performed security tasks in the Pristina Corps in 1998 and 1999, and what was the organisation of the security organs in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, there were military security service organs of the Pristina Corps, as well as military security service organs of the command of the military district of Pristina, and the security organs of the 14th Counter-intelligence Group, which was directly subordinated to the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us how was the military security section in the Pristina Corps organised? What was its structure?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The structure of the security organs of the Pristina Corps was such that all corps military security organs were under the chief of security of the Pristina Corps. In each brigade there was a separate person in charge of security, as well as in each independent battalion. Due to the complex security situation, in mid-1998 the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of the FRY strengthened the security organs of the Pristina Corps. As of that moment, the organs of the military security service existed in all organisational units down to combat groups and border posts of the Army of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us about the functional structure of the security section of which you were in charge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The functional structure of the security section comprised the counter-intelligence sector and the security sector. The counter-intelligence sector would monitor, intercept, and disclose any enemy intelligence activity against the commands and institutions belonging to the FRY army. Its task was also to prevent any terrorist activity against the commands, institutions, and units of the army. The staff security section dealt with things that had to do with the day-to-day workings of the staff. They would also propose pre-emptive command measures in the security field. They were also in charge of technical guidance over the military police units of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the manning levels in the Pristina Corps security bodies in 1998 and 1999 specifically?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, the security bodies of the Pristina Corps in 1998 and 1999 had manning levels well beyond their establishment. There were the schools and military academies of the FRY. Some of the students saw their education stopped, come to an abrupt halt, because there was a seconded to the security organs of the Pristina corps to help out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What are the competencies of powers of the military security service vis-à-vis the military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The military security service is technically in charge of the military police and its work, the technical aspects of the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the security sector and the security organs, do they have the right to order the use of military police units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Security officers have no power to order even a single unit that is part of the Army of the FRY, and that includes the military police units. The unit commander was the only person who had the right to order the use of these units, the commander of that unit that the military police units were part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the Pristina Corps specifically, which military police unit was that in 1999, and I believe earlier on as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Under the establishment and structure of the Pristina Corps, in 1998 and 1999, the units of the Pristina Corps had an A Class battalion, more specifically, the 52nd Military Police Battalion. There were two Military Police Companies as well, the 549 Motorised Brigade, that's where it was at, and there was a company of the military police in the 152nd Motorised Brigade. Under the war establishment, all A Class brigades of the Pristina Corps each had a military police company attached to it. However, in those brigades where there were no such units prior to 1998 and 1999, before a state of war was declared, these were simply mobilised so they were now part of those brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In terms of command, who was the superior or the commander of the 52nd Battalion military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of command, and this applied to all the units, the level of a brigade or independent battalion, and this included the 52nd Battalion of the military police, the sole right to command these units was held by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the specific obligations of the security organs of the units of the Pristina Corps vis-à-vis their commanders?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The organs of the military security service in terms of establishment are subordinated to the units of which they are a part. In a technical sense, the direct superior of the military security service of the superior command, superior to the unit in which this body or organ happens to be, is in charge. The obligations of the military security service were to gather intelligence, to make appropriate assessments, and to analyse. They were also to propose specific measures to unit commanders, as well as to document any activity undertaken by the enemy, as well as to take pre-emptive action in order to keep any negativities from occurring in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us this: What were the fundamental tasks of the military security service in 1998 and 1999 when it came specifically to terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Discovering, documenting, and intercepting any terrorist activity in and against the commands, units, and institutions, which applied to both peacetime and war time, and remained throughout one of the three fundamental counter-intelligence tasks in terms of protecting the actual units. Specifically, speaking of 1998 and 1999, the military security service units of the Pristina Corps were particularly busy detecting, documenting, and intercepting any terrorist activity in and against the commands, the units, and the institutions of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout 1998 and 1999, did the military security service deal with the terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, due to the apparent danger posed by the terrorists vis-à-vis the commands of our units and institutions, and particularly when it came to our units in the border belt facing the Republic of Albania. Another reason was obvious terrorist activity by the Albanian terrorists aimed at the commands, units, and members of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the security sector of the Pristina Corps, did it have any obligation to report to its superior commands?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A security sector of the Pristina Corps was under an obligation to continually report both in a vertical and in a horizontal sense. When I say vertical reporting, what exactly do I mean? The security sector was under an obligation to continually keep reporting to its own direct superior, the superior's security organ within the hierarchy, which was the security department of the 3rd Army. Likewise, throughout 1998 and up until the point at which a state of war was declared, the security service of the Pristina Corps Command would send telegrams in addition to the security section of the 3rd Army, also to the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of the FRY. From the beginning of the NATO aggression, the security service would only report to its direct superior which was the security section of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Why was there this discrepancy in terms of this chain of reporting which came about in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1998 when it came to the security situation that prevailed in the Republic of Serbia, if you forget about Kosovo, the situation was relatively peaceful. The security sector of the Pristina Corps Command had received orders from the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of the FRY, in addition to the security sector of the 3rd Army, to also inform about any of the intelligence that it received, the staff administration of the 3rd Command. The reason probably being the security administration of the Supreme Command staff wanted to familiarise itself with the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija over the shortest time possible. And we need to bear in mind the fact that the situation was worsening on a daily basis. The security sector of the Pristina Corps, ever since the start of the NATO aggression, no longer reported to the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of the FRY, as ordered by the administration itself. If you want my opinion, the reasons probably were as follows: Firstly, a state of war had been declared. Secondly, the entire staff of the Supreme Command was now facing numerous problems as well as the security administration itself, therefore, the security administration tried to take things back to what the regulations actually stated. It would not be receiving reports directly from the Pristina Corps but, rather, through the security administration of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In addition to the security sector of the Pristina Corps, were there any other players in the field of military security that were reporting to these superior commands?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: By all means, in addition to the security sector of the Pristina Corps, as I pointed out earlier, there existed also the security organs of the command of the Pristina military district. In a technical sense, these were also subordinated to the security sector of the 3rd Army. Again, in a technical sense, they reported to the security sector of the 3rd Army. Likewise, in Kosovo and Metohija throughout 1998 and 1999, there was the 14th Counter-intelligence Group which, both in a technical sense and in terms of hierarchy, was subordinated to the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of the FRY because it was one of its components. The security organs belonging to the 14th Counter-intelligence Group were permanently reporting directly to the security administration General Staff of the Army of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How exactly does one report to a superior command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There are several regulations that are in force describing the procedure for this. When it comes to horizontal reporting by a command organ, this comprises briefing at collegium meetings attended by commanders of the relevant units. If there is a situation that poses a direct threat to that unit, in that case, the security organs would report to the unit commanders or inform the unit commanders by an Official Note. When it came to vertical reporting, the organs of the military security service, throughout 1998 and in the first half of 1999 up until the cessation of combat activities in Kosovo, every day would send a telegram to the security administration of the General Staff, up until the end of March that is, of the Army of the FRY. And they continually reported to the security sector of the 3rd Army. Later on what was conveyed in these telegrams would have to be backed by other documents specified by the regulations governing the work of the military security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you acquaint us with the structure of those reports of the security section sent to superior commands?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, the security section of the Pristina Corps Command would daily, by telegram, inform their immediate superiors in terms of the security hierarchy. Such telegrams contained three units, so to speak. The first one had to do with the security situation at state borders. The second had to do with the security situation in the territory. And the third concerned itself with the security situation in the units, commands, and institutions of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you start working on security matters in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professionally speaking, I started working on the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija in 1990. And it went on until I -- for as long as I worked in the military security service of the Army of Yugoslavia in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the key factors influencing the change for the worst in terms of the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Many events which took place in Kosovo and Metohija in the recent or more distant past have their cause and effect. They did not come about as a result of political antagonism and changes in society, but they were, rather, an expression of a century long wish of Albanian separatists to see Kosovo and Metohija depart from the FRY and Serbia and to have it annexed to the greater Albanian state that was supposed to be created in the Balkans. I will refer to a number of key events which had a direct impact on the worsening of the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija. In 1982, in Germany, several militant political Albanian parties united, such as the Kosovo Party for the Socialist Republic of Kosovo in the FRY, then the Communist Marxist Leninist Party of Kosovo, as well as the People's Red Front. By uniting these illegal extremist Albanian parties, the national movement for the Republic of Kosovo was created. In the ore of their political activity was their wish to see Kosovo and Metohija become a republic of the Yugoslav Federation. Between 1982 and 1990, there were several isolated incidents in terms of terrorist activity in Kosovo carried out by small terrorist groups which, in hierarchical terms, did not share any links between each other. Another reason for the worsening of the security situation in Kosovo happened on the 2nd of July, 1990. Albanian separatists in Kacanik illegally proclaimed the Republic of Kosovo and elected its government headed by Bujar Bukosi. That government was active and working in Germany. Its task was to provide financial and logistical support for the project that was supposed to be implemented later on in 1998 and 1999. When the illegal assembly of the Republic of Kosovo was elected, it was decided that military and police forces need to be established. It was their belief that they needed 42.000 armed people in Kosovo to achieve their desired goal. During that session, the basic outline of the army structure was drawn up with operational zones which coincided with the operative zones from 1988 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- during which time there were extensive activities by the KLA. Security organs of the FRY managed to arrest 14 people belonging to the so-called Ministry of Defence of the illegal Republic of Kosovo. In their statements, they acknowledged the change of the national movement for the Republic of Kosovo and that they were as of that moment being called the movement for independent Kosovo. This marked a political change in their agenda. Kosovo was no longer supposed to be a separate republic in the SFRY but their new goal was to see Kosovo completely secede. Next key moment is in 1994 when the national movement for Kosovo made certain steps to meet the conditions necessary for what was to come about in 1998. They drew up a document called the strategics and tactics of the liberation war. In two volumes they worked out in detail their guerilla tactic that were -- that was supposed to be put in place in 1998. One could hear of the KLA for the first time in December 1994. A communiqué was issued to a number of people in Pristina by which they informed the public in Kosovo that they were behind the assassination of Lutvi Ajvazi, who was a retired member of the security forces. They also acknowledged that there were other terrorist acts in Kosovo committed by their members. Their first public appearance, so to say, was marked in 1995 at the funeral of Halit Becaj, a killed terrorist in the village of Laus. As of that moment onwards, the KLA became a part of reality in Kosovo and Metohija. I wanted to stress in particular the next key moment. After the crisis in Albanian in 1996 because of the savings scheme which collapsed, basically all state institutions caved in, including their army and the police. During that period, basically all weapons depots in Albania were broken into and weapons and equipment of the Albanian army were taken by bandits in the north of Albania. There is official data compiled by the UN on the number of weapons and assets stolen. By end 1997 and early 1998, those weapons found their way across the border into Kosovo and Metohija illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 15, line 3, that seems to be all right in the transcript now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us something about the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija in early 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The key moments which were the cause of the worsening situation in Kosovo-Metohija that year were actually two events. First, in February 1998, a terrorist group led by Adem Jashari that was active in the area of Drenica and it focused its activities on the villages of Donja and Gornja Prekaze, carried out -- before I go to that, in addition to that terrorist group, there was also a terrorist group in Jablanica in Metohija. Those two terrorists groups, throughout 1997, were the best known for their brutality and intensity of terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija. The terrorist group commanded by Jashari in February in Likosane from ambush attacked a vehicle of the minister of the interior of Serbia, on which occasion they killed four policemen and wounded two. In the ensuing clash during that night due to poor visibility and general chaos, the attack was repelled. And then by subsequent MUP activity, Adem Jasari's house was surrounded in Prekaze. He was liquidated on that occasion. The liquidation of Adem Jashari is very important because the Albanian separatists chose to use solely forceful means to achieve their proclaimed goals. The other event that worsened the situation in 1998 took place in early March. The Main Staff of the so-called KLA with its seat in Switzerland transferred parts of its staff to the north of Albania. Some staff members were also brought over the border into Kosovo and Metohija. Those members were Hashim Thaqi, Ramush Haradinaj, and Kadri Veseli. The task of that part of the main staff of the KLA was to organise and unite the several terrorist groups in Kosovo and to introduce hierarchy and subordination among them, as well as to set the conditions needed to carry out an armed rebellion of Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was done by the command of the Pristina Corps in such a security situation in early 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Believing that the overall security situation in Kosovo is growing more complex, the command of the Pristina Corps in March 1998 issued a decision to use several combat groups which were supposed to leave the barracks in order to provide assistance to the border authorities in order to prevent any further incursions of terrorists from Albania. Whereas parts of those groups were also supposed to be deployed to different roads between Kosovo -- inside Kosovo and Metohija, so as to prevent any danger to logistics and supplies being brought to the various units of the FRY that were in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D006-3159. Your Honours, could we please provide the witness with a hard copy of this and other documents so that it would be easier for him to read and this may speed things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a 65 ter Defence document 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's the first document in your binder. The date is the 18th of April, 1998. It's a document of the 3rd Army Command. Witness, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a telegram of the 3rd Army Command. It was dispatched to the 14th Counter-intelligence Group of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You actually received this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at paragraph 2. Can you comment on the, or, rather, bullet point number 2, item number 2, can you comment on the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You see that this is a telegram from April 1998. And the second paragraph identifies the organisers of the import of illegal weapons from Albania into Kosovo. It also talks about the role of the Haradinaj family in the village of Glodjane. The information applies to both 1998 and 1999 throughout. Glodjane was sort of a halfway station in this whole business of bringing illegal weapons from Albania into Kosovo and Metohija, and from Glodjane these weapons were transported to other terrorist strong holds across Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about the second to last and last paragraphs of this telegram?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The second to last paragraph talks about information that the security organs received on a number of different occasions. It talks about the village of Jablanica which was the second most important terrorist strong hold in Djakovica municipality. It tells us there was a group of 180 Albanian citizens there training the local population. This all tells us what would be happening later on and escalating in May and June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about page 1, could you please comment on paragraph 3 where it says that some terrorists were being illegally infiltrated from other places abroad such as Turkey?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We had reliable information indicating that among the so-called Kosovo liberation army ranks throughout 1998 and 1999, there were certain mercenaries, as well, fighting from the countries of the Arab world. I will be talking about other documents which you will probably be using, but here it says that three Arabs and two Muslims from the Kostris region were illegally infiltrated to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can we please have this document exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out in the English version the date is different. It says 1996. So I just wanted to maybe have clarification on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I've noticed that. The original appears to be 1998 when it's examined more closely, and the contents seem to suggest 1998 rather than 1996, including the date in the third paragraph, which is a 1998 date. So I think we can take it as a 1998 document, wrongly translated as 1996 in the English version. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00725.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my learned friend and the Chamber too. Could we please have D008-3706. 65 ter Defence document 573.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is tab 1 in your binder, Mr. Stojanovic. I would like to know about this position that is being put forward here. We are talking about the security section of the Pristina Corps telegram dated the 31st of May, 1999 -- 1998. I want to know your opinion about paragraph 2 of this telegram.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 talks about information indicating that the terrorists were fortifying their positions in some of their villages that were ethnically pure Albanian villages. They were moving women and children out of these villages and taking them further into their territory. This was the kind of information received on a daily basis. These terrorists were continually manipulating the population and moving them about all the time, the purported objective being to better prepare for their defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If you could please just comment on this: We have Colonel Djindjic who apparently signed the document. Do you have anything to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1998, he was seconded to the security sector of the Pristina Corps as were other high-ranking officers from the security department of the 3rd Army. In this specific case, the telegram was signed by Colonel Slobodan Djindjic who was the deputy chief of the security section of the 3rd Army. At this point in time, he was seconded to this unit. In nine out of ten cases I, as chief, would sign these documents. But he was my direct superior, and I was probably elsewhere at this point in time, so we see that he was the officer who signed this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we please have this document Exhibited. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00726.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-3252. 65 ter Defence document 132.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 2 for you, General. This is a telegram of the security sector of the Pristina Corps dated the 10th of June, 1998. Could you please first of all comment on paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is another telegram dealing with intelligence that was indicated in the previous one, the terrorists were moving the women, children, and the elderly out of the villages in the Djakovica municipality leaving only terrorists behind who were preparing for armed actions. Furthermore, this telegram shows that a secret KLA military police was set up in Djakovica, and they were mobilising people. The reference here is to groups of men who the terrorists leaders in civilian clothes were sending about town and they were trying to persuade all Albanians to join the terrorists staffs of the KLA. And if I may, towards the end of this telegram, there is information indicating that for one particular battalion of the 549 Brigade, five Albanian soldiers fled who had previously received a transfer from Valjevo. Generally speaking, before and during 1998 and 1999, units of the Pristina Corps were being reinforced by soldiers from training centres across Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this please be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00727.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D006-3255, Defence document 133.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram of the security sector of the Pristina Corps dated 12th of June, 1998. Could you please comment on paragraph 3, page 1?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. I'm looking at Article 3 of the document before us, it tells us that the people of Korenica village in Djakovica municipality were prepared to request protection from the VJ. They got in touch with the security organs of the Pristina Corps precisely for that purpose. We conveyed to them our position and said that the condition for their protection, which we would be providing, was them not joining any KLA terrorists units and then handing over their weapons. I know that the action came to nothing. We are talking about June and July 1998 when several Albanian villages throughout Kosovo and Metohija publicly expressed a desire to issue a guarantee to the Pristina Corps that they would not be joining any units of the KLA. However, they requested protection from the VJ. They wanted the VJ to protect them and to protect them from any abuse by the terrorists who sometimes came to those villages. There were cases like that occurring, and there were several villages across Kosovo and Metohija that negotiated with VJ in order to hand over their weapons of their own free will. Nevertheless, the terrorists brutally punished some of those people involved in those negotiations. You might say that the initiative was nipped in the bud by the actions of the KLA. Had this got off the ground, this initiative, I'm quite certain that violence in Kosovo and Metohija would never have escalated to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May this please be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00728.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence document D006-3260.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 4 in your binder, Mr. Stojanovic. Defence document 134. What we are looking at is a telegram by the security sector of the Pristina Corps, and the date is the 13th of June, 1998. Sir, could you please comment on paragraph 5. This is page 2 in the English version. It says the villages around Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is tab 4; have you got that? It reads, the paragraph starts like this: "Such intelligence as is available indicates ..." And then it goes on to say villages around Prizren. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The document talks about the fact that in the villages around Prizren, the terrorists were seising all-terrain vehicles from the local population in order to transport their own men. And then in the villages of Gjakove municipality, they were looting houses that had been abandoned. If I may just add this, we are talking about May and June, that's the time-frame, the time when the terrorists declared a mobilisation of all able-bodied young men who would then be joining the units of the KLA. At that point time, the Pristina Corps recorded many cases of torture and inhumane treatment of Albanians who chose to remain loyal to the authorities in cases where these Albanians were refusing to join the terrorist units of the KLA. So these terrorists were seising, by force, all-terrain vehicles from the locals. They would break into their homes to tell them that the least they had to do was provide a weapon, a rifle for their purposes, and their family members should be joining the KLA and their units. So this document talks about precisely that period of time and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move down the page, a single paragraph down the page, where it talks about the 12th of June. That one and the last paragraph on this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. The last paragraph talks about information covering the attacks being carried out by the Albanian terrorists against Serb enclaves in Kosovo and Metohija, the small ones actually, and those with a mixed population, both Serb and Albanian. There was a lot of information indicating that there was a gradual ethnic cleansing effort of that particular area and primarily of central Kosovo. The last paragraph of this document tells us specifically about the village of Rudnik, continually under the sniper fire of the terrorists, where the house of recently murdered Blagoje Jovanovic from Leocine was set on fire. During that night, another 11 Serbian houses had been set ablaze. And the fate of four people from that village is unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May the document please be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D00729.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D011-3437. It is document 1806 of the Defence. By your leave, Your Honour, I would like to add this document on our 65 ter list. It is an information note concerning an event in the Radanovic border post area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you had time to consider this, Ms. Petersen?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I don't have an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be added, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of the document is D011-3347.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, can you you comment on this document briefly?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This information note deals with a border incident in the area of the Radanovic border post dated the 15th of June, 1998. On that occasion, an illegal entry was prevented of a large group of Albanian terrorists from Albania. Among the documents and personal IDs found on the liquidated terrorists, there were also documents found belonging to a Norwegian journalist by the name of Pal Refsdal, born 9 September 1963 in Kongsvinger, as well as a camera. This indicated that not only terrorists were using illegal channels to enter Kosovo, but also foreign nationals, journalists, as well as workers of international humanitarian organisations according to our information. This was very difficult to comprehend, having in mind that any journalist could have asked for official accreditation, which could be obtained by -- from Serbian organs in order for them to legally spend periods of time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the information you have from that time concerning journalists and members of humanitarian organisations as well as various NGOs, did you have any information on their subversive activities directed against the FRY and the Republic of Serbia and Kosovo and Metohija in addition to their illegal entries in co-operation with separatist organisations and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in our military security service documents, there is a lot of information about such employees of international humanitarian organisations and journalists. This information concerns their objectivity in work and reporting. They were quite inclined towards the KLA, and we also have certain information about their activities in the General Staff or the Main Staff of the KLA during that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00730.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have D006-3263. It is number 135 of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your tab 6, General. This will be a telegram of the security section of the Pristina Corps dated the 16th of June, 1998. Please comment on the first paragraph of this telegram.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of this telegram which is related to the first one, we have the following information: That there was information that the MUP had about the action in the Koranovic [phoen] border post area. This information indicated that a Norwegian journalist was wounded. His name is Refsdal Pal who is undergoing medical treatment in the illegal Siptar hospital in the territory of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you comment please on the penultimate paragraph of this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph, it is stated that there was an exchange of information with the Prizren SUP about armed terrorists who have appeared in the area of Sopot village and that they have pressured locals - and I need to mention here that it was an ethnically pure village - they pressured locals into leaving the village. And the Djakovica SUP has information that terrorists are planning to set ambushes in the very area where the 52nd Military Police Battalion is deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00731.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next could we please have D006-3155. It is Defence number 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And your tab 7, General. It's another telegram of the security section of the Pristina Corps dated the 23rd [as interpreted] of June, 1998. At the bottom of your page 1 - which in English should be page 2 - the one before last paragraph, please comment. It begins with the words "using electronic surveillance."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph of the first page states certain information about something we have already referred to, that is, the five Muslim soldiers who fled their unit after being relocated to Kosovo from Valjevo. By using electronic surveillance, we learned that those soldiers were in the terrorist stronghold in the village of Drenovac, Orahovac municipality. They made some phone calls to their relatives in which they were trying to talk their relatives into relocating to the Republic of Albania. Also, instruction was given to them to tell the authorities there that the Army of Yugoslavia had forced them to kill innocent civilians. This was in order to claim political asylum. This was yet another propaganda activity of which there were many in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether we have the right date for this document. It is the 28th of June, 1998. I apologise if I misspoke. I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00732.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Your Honour, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now, and we resume in half an hour. A Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, were you informed in early July about the situation in Metohija, especially in the municipality of Orahovac? Did you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In several zones in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, the overall security situation was quite grave. One of such areas was the general area of Malisevo and Orahovac. During 1998 and especially in the first part of that year, Orahovac as a town was completely surrounded by Albanian terrorists and there was this constant danger that the town will remain completely blocked by the Albanian terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D006-2501.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 8, General. Defence number 106. This document is dated the 8th of July, 1998, by the speaker of the Municipal Assembly of Orahovac, Mr. Andjel Kolasinac. Did you know that this letter was sent and were you familiar with its contents in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D008-3730.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram of the security section of the Pristina Corps dated the 17 July 1998. Please comment paragraphs 2, 3, 4, and 5 on this page.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this telegram there is information about an event which took place on the 16th of July, 1998, when our border authorities in the area of Kosare prevented an attempt of illegal entry by a group of civilians and armed terrorists from Kosovo to Albania. What is particularly noteworthy is that among those arrested on that occasion, there was a foreign national, Sally Becker, born 29 March 1960. She introduced herself to the police as a person belonging to a humanitarian organisation. She had a Motorola, a two-way hand-held radio, on her and according to her statement, she was in contact with representatives of the humanitarian organisations present in the north of Albania. She also admitted to having spent some time in terrorist headquarters in the villages of Junik, Nivokaz, Dobros, and Smonica. She also had a piece of paper we are the names of Naim Maljoku and Lum Haxhiu who were well-known commanders of the terrorist headquarters. In addition to representatives of the media in 1998, there were illegal crossings between Albania and Kosovo by members of international humanitarian organisations. Although, according to my information at the time, there was no prohibition for any international humanitarian organisation staff which would limit them to enter Kosovo and Metohija, provided they had legal permission by our authorities. The way they tried to enter Kosovo territory raises certain doubts as to their intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is the bottom of page 1 in your version, please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In one of the paragraphs of this document it is stated that on the 17th of July, Albanian terrorists attacked a Serb village called Zociste, exclusively populated by Serbs in the municipality of Orahovac. At the moment when this report was written, one could hear shots from Orahovac itself according to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please turn to your page 2 towards the middle, application of electronic surveillance measures. It is the last paragraph in English. Please comment.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is stated that by the application of electronic reconnaissance measures, information was received that in Bajram Curi, a town in the north of Albania, there were two known terrorists who are planning to cross the state border and introduce 100.000 Swiss francs into Kosovo as well as 11 radio sets, uniforms, medicine, and equipment for the terrorists and the territory of Stimlje municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page in the English version, which is also your page 3, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please comment. In the English, it is the last paragraph of page 3, and in your version it is the third from the top, "the latest information," it says.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we received this information as an exchange of information procedure with the security service in Kosovo and Metohija. It is indicated that medical supply for the use of terrorists in the so-called Baranski Lug which is between the municipalities of Decani and Djakovica, that said supplies are being transported by vehicles using -- the vehicles belonging to the Medecines Sans Frontieres and the ICRC through Grabovica where they were taken over by members of the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, what has this document to do with the case we are trying? Now, this is part of a bigger question, that is, the amount of time that is being spent on matters that aren't central to our case. Could you assist us with what you see is important about this document in the case we are trying, which is an indictment concerning events commencing some nine months after any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the year of 1998 is a period that has to do with knowledge of what happened and how things came about. Much of the OTP case was about that. We, the Defence, are now trying to show how the reporting was done in Kosovo and Metohija starting back in 1998. There are some important elements there. For example, regarding the way the security forces worked and the disproportion use of force; how the rural republic public was being made aware of going on in Kosovo; and then later the Kosovo Verification Mission, how it went about its work, what it had to do with the Kosovo Liberation Army, and how it misused its mandate, all of which, I believe, is evidence that must be evaluated by the Trial Chamber in this case. We also have to look at the media, how the media worked. We have to look at how civilians were misused in 1998 and 1999. Who was in charge of that and how exactly was this done? I believe this constitutes knowledge that is relevant in this case in terms of evaluating evidence that we have seen so far and evidence that is still to be produced in this trial. We have had a long sequence of exhibits in relation to this period, the five-stage plan, and everything that when on later on before reaching October and the arrival of the Kosovo Verification Mission. These same persons then testified about what they did later on in Albania and Macedonia and were offering up witnesses who would be making statements to the ICTY. I do believe that this is highly significant in terms of actually judging the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, there is another thing. Most of these documents were used previously in the Milutinovic case, some of these documents. And some, especially those in relation to later on, are documents that are being used for the very first time in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we are not persuaded by what you say, that the material you are presently canvassing is important in our case. We have received, and are prepared to receive from you, a limited amount of general background information. We have certainly been prepared and will need to look more closely at what is being advanced concerning the activities of the Kosovo Verification Mission, but those activities did not start until much later in 1998 and our primary interest will be in 1999. Now, what you are dealing with here are documents which are painting a picture about events that are of no interest in the trial we have to deal with at all. You have spent some minutes dealing with this last interest that some medical supplies were being brought in to a dig. That is just completely irrelevant to anything we have to deal with. What we are becoming very concerned about is the perception of the Defence as to its case is losing sight of the indictment in this case. This Chamber is not going to try the rights and wrongs of the battle that seems to have been fought over a year and a half or so between the Kosovo Liberation Army, as it came to be known, and the forces of the Government of Serbia. We are going to be focusing on those events which are in the indictment. Now, we will not confine you to giving evidence only about the period of the indictment, but every time you are dealing with matters 9 or 12 months earlier, which this witness has done now for over an hour and a half, you need to ask the question, how is this important to the Defence case? And the Chamber, for its part, is not persuaded that the importance of what you have dealt with is of such significance in this case that it can't have learnt all about these matters from the transcript in the Milutinovic case which is already an exhibit. You have spent an hour and a half dealing with detail which is all canvassed in a much shorter time in the Milutinovic case. Now, what I'm saying is not to stop you dealing with these matters at all, but it is to put to you that you are giving to them an importance and an emphasis and you are spending time way beyond their possible relevance in our case. Now, if you would, as you look at your case from now on, try and be more clear as to whether a particular document or a particular event is going to advance your case in answer to this indictment, and if you'll answer to yourself, Well, it's part of the background picture; then ask yourself very carefully, is it adequately dealt with in the transcript already? And if it is, there's no need to repeat it. If it is not, there might be something more that you need to deal with, deal with that, but don't go over the whole story again. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document please be received, the last one that the witness commented on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber does not see that it is sufficiently relevant, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, this is a document from the Milutinovic trial. It was exhibited there. I was merely trying to point out a number of matters that didn't have anything to do with what preceded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You realise, Mr. Djurdjic, we are not trying the accused that are on trial in the Milutinovic case; we are trying Mr. Djordjevic. And it is an indictment focused on his conduct and focused on his conduct over a period of time which is over nine months later than this document. There may be, in the events of this period in 1998, a general picture that you want to paint for us and which it will be important for us to understand, but this document that you are offering doesn't tell us anything of relevance to the indictment against Mr. Djordjevic. So just because it was used in the Milutinovic trial, doesn't mean that it's going to help us try the case against your client. It might have had some relevance to some of the other accused in that case. We don't see it as having a sufficient relevance in this case to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but I would like to receive further instructions from you. We had Mr. Crosland here who testified to this time-period and the period that preceded this period, fields being set on fire, internal displacement, disproportionate use of force; the whole period up to the 28th of March. One of the witnesses, who I believe is relevant in terms of what the Prosecution put forward, in 1998 and those periods of time, one of the sources of information to counter Mr. Crosland's evidence, and provide the Chamber with a different perspective, this is the witness we are dealing with today, and we are not just talking about how KDOM continued to work. They came before the Kosovo Verification Mission, but a lot of other evidence about internally displaced people, about the disproportionate use of force in 1998, and so on and so forth. We have seen the evidence of the OTP, and now we are trying to counter their evidence by our own evidence. That's what we are trying to achieve. Had we not spoken so much about 1998 in the Prosecution case, then I hardly think we would be giving it so much attention in our own case, had we only stuck to 1999 to begin with. But we have the Human Rights Watch, Witness Abrahams who testified about what went on in Albania from 1996 onwards; I can't remember each and every one ever the OTP's witnesses, but they testified to these circumstances. And then particularly the international media, how they covered the situation, international humanitarian organisations, plenty of documents have been admitted in various ways showing us how they worked, the representers of these international humanitarian organisations. That is the reason that we -- well, I don't know, how are we could counter such evidence produced by the OTP unless we reflects on 1998 as well? We lost a lot of time during the OTP's case discussing 1998. I do feel I have to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you are misunderstanding the thrust of our comments. We are not saying that there is no relevance to your case of events in 1998. Very early in this trial the view was urged on us by both counsel, that is Prosecution and Defence, that the events in 1999 could not be viewed in isolation and we had to be aware of the events particularly in 1998 that had led to the time in the indictment. For that reason, out of respect for the views urged on us by counsel, we have heard evidence both from the Prosecution and from the Defence about the period in 1998 and even earlier. We have done so, though, if you look at it, in a general overall perspective. We have not gone into a detailed history of what may have been the struggle or events in 1998 at all. We have been looking at the general picture. Our constant call both to the Prosecution and to the Defence has been to concentrate on the period of the indictment, and to be not misled by the possible relevance of the general picture into thinking that we are going to be determining the guilt or innocence of your client by trying all the events that occurred a year, or more even, earlier than the events with which he is charged. Now, this particular document to us is reaching down to trying to look at detailed events over nine months before the indictment period. The fact that a group of civilians came across a border, the fact that among them was one woman who claimed to be a member of an humanitarian organisation, the fact that there may have been a member of the international media crossing a border without normal customary formalities, the fact that an international organisation or two may have been providing medical supplies to a dig, how are any of those matters going to help us determine the guilt or innocence of your client as charged in this indictment? The thing that comes nearest to anything of relevance in this document is that there was an attack on the village of Zociste, I'm not sure of the pronunciation. A Serb village. That's the nearest to anything of relevance in this case. And the point is that without the document we've heard about that attack, what this witness knows about it. So we ask again, how is this document going to help us? I've stopped you here because it's just clearly that you are going to be going through every document this witness might talk about, about events in 1998, and the point we are making is that some or many of those documents are not going to help us at all. This witness, no doubt, will be able to tell us some matters that are of some relevance to us. We want to hear those. But we don't want to canvass the whole history of 1998 as this witness knows it, because it's just going too far into matters of little or no relevance. Does that help you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I understood, Your Honour. I will be dealing with some documents very swiftly. I will be skipping some and I will be addressing some that I believe might contribute. Thank you. Could we please have D006-3163.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the first paragraph, Witness. It is your tab 10, another telegram of the Pristina Corps Command dated 18 July. Can you comment on the first paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This telegram has do with the action undertaken by the terrorists against Orahovac between the 17th and the 18th of July, 1998, when they occupied most of the town and took 30 Serb locals in an unknown direction. They also seised a large quantity of medical material.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have Prosecution document 4188 on the 65 ter list. This is an information note of the security service and its Prizren centre in 1998, the 1st of August, concerning the attack on Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, did you used to receive such information from the state security administration in 1998 and 1999, and did you have any exchanges of information between your intelligence section of the Pristina Corps and the state security service?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During 1998 and 1999, we regularly exchanged information with the state security service in Kosovo and Metohija, although I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D006-3170.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is the 14th tab in your binder. Defence number 120. This is a letter that was sent as a telegram by the security section of the Pristina Corps on 24 July 1998 to the General Staff security administration in the VJ, security department of the 3rd Army, as well as the security organ of the 14th Counter-intelligence Group. What is this document, and why was it drawn up? What was the situation like at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This telegram of 24 July 1998, it was drafted following a request of the security head in the Pristina Corps Command. It gives an overview of security in late July 1998. Among other things, there is an assessed number of 25.000 armed terrorists. We can also find the security section's opinion as to what their further plans will be. At that time, regular life and work in Kosovo and Metohija ground to a halt when all of the roads were basically blocked by the terrorists. At this point in time, the situation was the most complex and difficult one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D011-3348.

utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what this map represents? Please comment.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the level of the security section, we kept a working map constantly plotting locations and information we had on the whereabouts and numbers of terrorists, as well as the territory under their control. On this map that was created in late June 1998, which I personally created, we can see precise locations of the terrorist groups in Albania -- in Kosovo and Metohija, as well as the locations of their brigades and operational zones in which those brigades were active. We also see the disposition of combat groups of the Pristina Corps in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please -- could we please have this document admitted.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they are in red. Those are the combat groups of the Pristina Corps. In blue we have the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm seeing roughly 14, then, combat groups of the Pristina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have time to count them, but these were their precise locations.

utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, that will be received.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the top of the map it says: "Disposition of the combat groups of the Pristina Corps and terrorist formations of the KLA in Kosovo and Metohija in mid-1998."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I'd like to thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could we also have you read out the key.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The key of this map says, in red, it says: "The forces of the VJ." And in blue: "Siptar terrorist forces and operational zones."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that my learned friend had the same question as I did. Very well, let us move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, after this period, we know that there were certain anti-terrorist activities that took place which were completed by late September and early October of that year. Can you tell us what the security situation was like in late September and early October 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the assessment we saw a moment ago, as well as on the assessment of other professional bodies between late July and late September 1998, there were several phases planned to carry out anti-terrorist operations carried out by security forces and the Army of the Republic of Yugoslavia. During that large operation, basically all significant Albanian terrorist strongholds were eliminated that we can see on the map. We also managed to completely break-up the terrorist composition of the KLA, and they were reduced to a number of small groups scattered about the mountainous terrain in Kosovo and Metohija. Since there were negotiations under way on the 13th of October, the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was signed, which, among other things, envisaged for all units which were brought in as reinforcements of the Pristina Corps be withdrawn from the area of Kosovo and Metohija. This was done. It was also envisaged that parts of combat groups be returned to their home garrisons, and that in the territory there should only be several combat groups in the border belt to the Republic of Albania with the task of assisting border units in order to prevent en masse entry of terrorists and weapons, as well as three combat groups along the road Pristina and Prizren at Dulje pass, which was a critical point, and another group on the road between Pristina and Pec in the Volujak region, and the third combat group which was I believe was in the area of Stimlje. All other forces under that agreement were withdrawn to the barracks of the VJ in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether this concluded any anti-terrorist measures by Serb forces and the army once the agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All anti-terrorist actions stopped after the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the KLA also cease its activities following the signing of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the agreement was signed and the MUP and army forces were withdrawn, and I also forgot to mention, I believe, that parts of MUP units also returned to their respective areas of deployment and that they only left a few check-points along certain roads. In this newly created situation, as we can see from numerous reports by command organs and the security section of the Pristina Corps, the terrorists used that situation to resupply and take up all positions in Kosovo and Metohija from which the security forces had withdrawn. They also continued unhindered supply of weapons and equipment. It can be seen from numerous intelligence section telegrams that they were preparing themselves for a spring offensive. In a way, the agreement enabled the terrorist staffs to consolidate and resupply for a renewed action against security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have Defence number 586.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your tab 18.

utterances.text: It is on your page 2, General, as well as in the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is stated in this item that terrorists also attacked business facilities in Kosovo and Metohija in addition to attacking security forces. In this document, an incident is mentioned where workers of the Bilacevac [phoen] mine were attacked as well as certain workers being kidnapped from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC

utterances.text: Your tab 19. This is a document of the 20th of October, 1998, a telegram by the security section of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have item 2 in both versions. I believe it is your page 2, General, and the same in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you see 2.2? Can you comment briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This corroborates my previous assertion. Two terrorist staffs leaders in Kosovo and Metohija who were active in the Dukadjin operational zone, Ibrahimaj [phoen] and Ramush Haradinaj, regrouped their terrorist formations, formed a number of smaller groups, and carried out abuse and intimidation of Albanians loyal to the Serb state as well as follow the activities of our security services focusing on roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
